question: Which set of conditions represents the standard autoclave (moist heat) sterilisation cycle used in hospital central sterile supply departments?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The standard autoclave cycle uses saturated steam at 121°C and 15 psi for 15 minutes. Moist heat kills by denaturing proteins and is the most reliable and widely used method for heat-stable items.

These are the conditions for a hot air oven (dry heat sterilisation), not an autoclave. Dry heat kills by oxidation and requires higher temperatures and longer exposure because air conducts heat less efficiently than steam.
Boiling at 100°C achieves disinfection, not sterilisation — it does not reliably kill bacterial endospores. Boiled instruments are therefore unsuitable for surgical use.

While 134°C / 30 psi / 3 minutes is a valid prevacuum (flash) cycle used for unwrapped instruments in emergencies, the standard cycle for wrapped instrument packs in CSSD remains 121°C / 15 psi / 15 minutes.

overallFeedback.feedback: The autoclave uses saturated steam under pressure: 121°C, 15 psi, 15 minutes. Distinguish this from dry heat (160°C / 60 min in a hot air oven) and boiling (100°C — only disinfects, does not sterilise).

121°C / 15 psi / 15 minutes is the gold standard. Biological indicators using Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores verify cycle efficacy. Remember: cleaning must always precede autoclaving to remove organic matter.
